There may be no better illustration of the critical and integral role the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has played in the history of our nation’s health than the timely juxtaposition of two anniversaries occurring this year – our nation’s 250th and the FDA’s 120th. That’s because this confluence underscores how, for nearly half of our nation’s existence, Americans have relied on, and benefited from, the FDA’s oversight of our food, medical products, veterinary products, cosmetics, and so much more. The FDA’s regulatory role began in 1906 with the passage of the Pure Food and Drugs Act, which authorized the Bureau of Chemistry—the FDA’s immediate predecessor—to regulate contaminated, misbranded, and dangerous foods and medicines. The agency did not receive its present name, the Food and Drug Administration, until 1930. Over time, the FDA’s basic law has been repeatedly amended, augmented, and strengthened in response to gaps or shortcomings, further enhancing the FDA’s essential role as the nation’s guardian of public health. pages.text: The federal budget process | USAGov Skip to main content The federal budget process Learn about the federal government’s budget process. Steps include the president creating the budget plan and Congress’s work creating funding bills for the president to sign. Annual funding areas Every year, the U.S. Congress begins work on a federal budget for the next fiscal year. The federal government’s fiscal year runs from October 1 of one calendar year through September 30 of the next. And the annual budget covers three spending areas: Mandatory spending - funding for Social Security, Medicare, veterans benefits, and other spending required by law. This typically uses over half of all funding. Discretionary spending - federal agency funding. Congress sets funding levels for these each year. This usually accounts for around a third of all funding. Interest on the debt - this usually uses less than 10 percent of all funding. Creating the U.S. federal budget The budget planning begins a year before the budget is to go into effect. Federal agencies create budget requests and submit them to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB). OMB refers to the agencies’ requests as it develops the budget proposal for the president. The president submits the budget proposal to Congress early the next year. Proposed funding is divided among 12 subcommittees, which hold hearings. Each handles funding for different government functions such as defense spending or energy and water. P. Cartier/Bridgeman/ACI By Javier Negrete Published February 15, 2024 The Roman Republic was booming in the beginning of the fourth century B.C. Wealthy and powerful, it had just defeated the Etruscan city of Veii, amassed an immense war chest, and doubled its territory. But then, out of the blue, the republic suffered the unthinkable: occupation by a Celtic people, the Gauls. This was the first time that Rome and Gaul would face off, but it would not be the last. Over the coming centuries, the Romans and the Gauls would clash many times. But this first defeat in 387 B.C. caused a collective trauma for Rome that lasted generations, shaping Roman attitudes toward all peoples from the north. ( How was Rome founded? Not in a day, and not by twins. ) Early encounters By 600 B.C. the Gallic people Insubres had already settled south of the Alps, where they founded Mediolanum (today’s Milan). It Just Got a Rare New Proof, but Some Still Long for a Simpler Solution Skip to main content Science | November 4, 2026 The Four-Color Theorem Has Haunted Mathematicians for Decades. It Just Got a Rare New Proof, but Some Still Long for a Simpler Solution The famous problem asks whether a map can be filled in with only four colors such that the same color never borders itself. It has been solved with the help of computers, but some experts suggest an elusive, short answer is out there The four-color theorem is simple to state: Given a contiguous map, is it possible to color each region with one of four colors such that no neighboring regions share a color? Vico Santos for Quanta magazine The four-color theorem is simple to state: Given a contiguous map, is it possible to color each region with one of four colors such that no neighboring regions share a color? Vico Santos for Quanta magazine The original version of this story appeared in Quanta magazine . Some math problems continue to haunt researchers long after they’ve been solved. A proof emerges, is even celebrated, and yet dissatisfaction lingers. SCIENCE LAELAPS The Jurassic Shield By Riley Black Published June 26, 2015 • 7 min read Some dinosaurs are better at hiding than others. There’s no single reason for their edge. Some were rare. Others too small to gain much notice from the paleontologists who were set on finding large, imposing specimens for museum centerpieces. Still more became preserved in slices of rock that haven’t gained the attention of the most famed quarries. Whatever the reasons, though, a big, heavily-armored dinosaur was able to escape the notice of paleontologists despite over a century of Jurassic exploration. North America’s Morrison Formation is a fossiliferous wonderland. Spectacular bonebeds dot its reach from Canada to Mexico, and it was one of the focal points for the great Bone Wars between O.C. Marsh and E.D. Cope in the late 19th century. Apatosaurus , Allosaurus , Camarasaurus , Diplodocus and more were the products of that feud. Strangest of all was Stegosaurus – a 30-foot-long quadruped with a tiny head, flashy plates along its back, and a set of four spikes jutting from the tip of its tail. Marsh named the bizarre animal in 1877, and ever since Stegosaurus has held the banner for the plated, spiky armored dinosaurs that were eventually replaced by ankylosaurs. Manual pendulum stamping was once popular in the 19th century. A decreased demand a result of the digital age has led the craft to nearly disappear. Yann Garin By Lauren Paige Richeson Published October 15, 2026 Long before our messages arrived with a buzz, a letter could introduce itself by touch. Without even glimpsing the handwriting inside, the paper itself announced a family name, a profession, a crest, or a ceremony—not merely a decoration, but a declaration. In Paris, one of the most refined ways to create that impression was with timbrage au balancier , or pendulum stamping. Developed in the 19th-century world of engraving and correspondence, the technique gave calling cards, invitations, letterheads, and envelope flaps something ordinary ink could not provide: a feeling. Everything from a coat of arms to a pair of initials could rise from the page in dense color and varying depths. But as correspondence slipped from paper to pixels and luxury printing pressed faster towards mechanized processes, the manual craft began to lose the world that sustained it. By 2022, the art rested in one last pair of hands: Éric Lejeusne, France’s last manual pendulum stamper, who was preparing to retire after decades in the trade

How did people survive? | National Geographic During the Little Ice Age, the Northern Hemisphere experienced long stretches of temperatures so cold that crops failed and rivers froze—like the Scheldt River, depicted here outside of Antwerp, Belgium, in a 1593 oil painting by Lucas van Valckenborch. Photograph by incamerastock, Alamy Stock Photo Premium ENVIRONMENT The Little Ice Age was brutal. How did people survive? From roughly the 16th to 19th centuries, much of the Earth was gripped by a persistent frigid cold. It left ripples through history—and some lessons for today’s climate crisis. By Kieran Mulvaney Published February 20, 2024 Thousands of people walking and playing across the frozen River Thames. Soldiers on horseback capturing ships stuck in the ice. Indigenous populations using snowshoes to outfox English interlopers. Accused witches put on trial as their communities struggled to explain crop failures and extreme cold. These were some of the images that define the Little Ice Age—a period of several centuries last millennium in which parts of the Northern Hemisphere grappled with a persistent cold. But what caused the Little Ice Age, how long did it last, how did people adapt to its frigid grip—and what lessons can we learn as we enter our own period of climatic change? ( Broken Baculum a Sign of Painful Ice Age Injury) What is the Little Ice Age—and what caused it? The Little Ice Age was not a true ice age—average cooling was probably only in the order of 0.5 degrees Celsius , or 1 degree Fahrenheit—nor was it consistently cold.

pages.text: The Little-Known Recording of Louis Armstrong Reciting 'The Night Before Christmas' Skip to main content “Bless whoever it was who came up with the idea,” jazz historian Dan Morgenstern says in a Smithsonian interview about Armstrong’s rendition of the holiday chestnut. Courtesy Continental Production Co. "This is Louis ‘Satchmo’ Armstrong,” the voice resounds, “talking to all the kids from all over the world at Christmastime.” With that, the trumpeter and singer tucks into a lyrical, buoyant reading of “The Night Before Christmas.” He hews to the words but makes them his own in a voice that glitters with joy. When the 69-year-old describes Santa’s “little round belly /that shook when he laughed like a bowl of jelly,” he breaks into a wheezy giggle that sounds like a truck rumbling to life at a green light. The poem, first published in 1823, would be Armstrong’s final commercial recording. Armstrong taped it on February 26, 1971, on a reel-to-reel recorder at his home in Queens, New York, during his last spell of good health. Four days later, he began an ill-advised two-week gig at the Waldorf Astoria that was followed by two heart attacks, one of them just two days after his final Waldorf show. On July 6, Armstrong died in his sleep, reportedly from heart failure. The recording was distributed that holiday season by cigarette-maker Lorillard, which pressed it onto a million 45-rpm records as giveaways for anyone who bought a carton of cigarettes. pages.text: The Remarkable, Amazing Stories of Route 66 Reflect the Twists and Turns of 100 Years of Americana Skip to main content There's More to That A Smithsonian magazine special report Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images via Library of Congress and public domain The famed Route 66 has had many lives . It emerged in an era when cars were new but roads were dangerous and intended for horses. But there were those who imagined a highway that would connect the cities of the Midwest to the West Coast — and Route 66 was born. During the Great Depression, the roadway helped migrants find their way to new jobs in the West. During World War II, it facilitated the transportation of munitions and armaments en route to the Pacific theater. Later, it became a busy thoroughfare for Americans wanting to explore their country. Storefronts, towns, gas stations, cafes and much more grew up along its edges. Then, as major interstates became the main byways for traveling Americans, Route 66 fell into obsolescence, becoming more a time capsule than roadway. Today, some of those roadside stops still exist, catering to tourists seeking a dose of unvarnished Americana. This episode chronicles the origin of the federal interstate system and how Route 66 fits into that history — before the massive tangle of highways and roads we know today were paved and packed with traffic. pages.description: Mom and pop motels once dominated American highways. Now, they're an endangered species
pages.text: The Rise and Fall of the Great American Motel Skip to main content The Wigwam Motel in Holbrook, Arizona, is one of the few remnants of America’s mid-20th century motel boom. Library of Congress In 1939, when John Steinbeck imagined Highway 66 as “the road of flight,” he evoked the crushing realities of Depression-era migrants who’d been pushed off their land by failing crops, relentless dust and heartless banks. Struggling to find some sense of home on the road, these environmental and economic refugees searched for hope against a backdrop of unfathomable loss. On the road to California, they’d rest and recuperate in army surplus tents, hastily constructed Department of Transportation camps and Sears Roebuck chicken-coop cabins . They could hardly imagine the surreal indulgences of the tourist road that would begin to emerge after World War II: renting a room built to resemble a country cottage and adorned with plastic flowers; snapping photos of a neon cactus glowing through half-drawn window shades; sleeping in a concrete tepee appropriated from Native American culture. They could, in short, never foresee the rise of the roadside motel. But after its heyday in the mid-20th century, the traditional mom and pop motel – once ubiquitous along American highways and byways – has largely slipped from the public imagination. Today’s road-tripper generally prefers lodging that boasts a professional website, guarantees a fast internet connection and promises easy-on-easy-off interstate access, leaving the older motels built along two-lane roads and numbered highways to go to seed.

More than two millennia ago, young girls from the Greek countryside used to travel every four years to the Sanctuary of Artemis at Brauron outside Athens, to participate in a mysterious rite of passage. They went there, one ancient participant enigmatically said, to “play the bear.” Guided by the priestesses of Artemis and out of sight of their fathers and brothers, the girls ran free, embodying the bear as part of a ritual that allowed them to shed their wildness and prepare for marriage. Painted cups found at the site that were possibly made by participants themselves show girls running and dancing. The opening ceremony won’t take place in a stadium but—bucking tradition—outside on the River Seine. For the Parade of Nations, boats carrying the participating teams will glide by an estimated 300,000 spectators congregated on the quays. Bathed in myth and memory, the Seine is the lifeblood of the city that sprang up on its banks. Along this “main street,” as Napoleon called it, photogenic Pari­sian landmarks are on proud display, oozing grandeur and majesty. It’s so cen­tral to the city’s existence that building numbers are linked to the river: Those on perpendicular streets begin their num­bering closest to the Seine, while on parallel streets building numbers ascend in the direction of the current. “For Parisians, there’s a strong historical and visceral attachment to the river,” says Pierre Rabadan, the deputy mayor in charge of sport, the Olympic and Paralympic Games, and the Seine. pages.text: The Surprising Secret Weapon Against Spotted Lanternflies | National Geographic Premium ANIMALS The Surprising Secret Weapon Against Spotted Lanternflies Early research suggests that a backyard plant might poison the invasive species. Scientists are studying a promising way to control the spread of the invasive spotted lanternfly with a common plant. Mark Mirko, Connecticut Public/Getty Images By Jason Bittel Published September 1, 2026 The spotted lanternfly is a large, visually striking insect that first showed up in the U.S. in 2014. In just over a decade, this invasive species has multiplied across the American Northeast, with new range expansions into the Midwest and South, bringing the total number of states where they can now be found to 19, as well as the District of Columbia. Not only do they feed on plant sap and harm trees, but spotted lanternflies also pose a threat to the grape and wine industry , among many other crops. Scientists have recently said that squashing them likely won’t make a dent in their populations. However, they may have stumbled upon a new weapon in the fight against the invasive species—one that just so happens to be critical habitat for monarch butterflies , an insect species perhaps as loved as the lanternfly is despised: Milkweed. When spotted lanternflies feed on the stuff, they have a tendency to drop dead. “We were planning to run the experiment for a week, except when we went back the next day, the majority of the lanternflies that were on milkweed were dead,” says Anne Johnson , a postdoctoral researcher at Michigan State University.

See more digitized stories from our archives here . I still recall the dredges and the bulldozers working in the red mangrove swamps near my father's house. I never thought their destruction was much of a loss. Mangroves were scrub: junk trees. The peculiar aerial roots, which, like spidery legs, prop the mangroves up in the mud, made the swamps seem forbidding. Swarms of mosquitoes and clicking, crablike creatures lurked within. The mud often stank. "No one likes the mangroves," John Steinbeck once wrote. And in Florida, until very recently, he was right. Few people complained as stands of mangroves along the state's southeast coast were replaced with sea-walled housing developments, hotels, and shopping plazas. What they found astounded them. By Robert Kunzig Published November 27, 2024 In February 2022, the reconstruction of the cathedral of Notre Dame in Paris was ready to begin. After the April 2019 fire, it had taken nearly three years to remove the debris and to shore up the damaged stone walls and ceiling vaults. If Notre Dame was to reopen in 2024, as French President Emmanuel Macron had decreed, it was urgent to begin rebuilding what had been lost—starting with the emblematic wooden spire that rises above the center of the church. An illustration shows what Duonychus tsogtbaatari might have looked like. Unlike its therizinosaur brethren, the new species had only two claws instead of three. Illustration by Masato Hattori By Riley Black Published March 25, 2025 Therizinosaurs were some of the strangest dinosaurs of all time. Descended from carnivores , the prehistoric reptiles were plant-eaters and had fuzzy feathered bodies, small heads with peg-like teeth in their jaws, bulbous stomachs that acted like fermenting vats for heaps of vegetation, and impressively large claws on each of their hands. Their build and claws have drawn comparisons to sloths, but some of these reptiles stood over 13 feet tall and weighed more than five tons. Now paleontologists have uncovered a therizinosaur that stands out even among its unusual relatives—because it’s missing a finger. Described in the journal iScience today, the new dinosaur comes from rocks in Mongolia’s Gobi Desert that are over 90 million years old. Back in 2012, paleontologists from the Mongolian Academy of Sciences initially unearthed parts of the spine, ribs, hips, and shoulders, and finally found two complete hands. Chang Lab / UCSF People with severe paralysis can struggle to communicate with others. While experimental brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have come a long way in being able to help them convey their thoughts , these technologies have generally been limited to either speech or movement . Now, scientists have developed a tool that can do both simultaneously. The implant, described in the journal Nature Neuroscience on September 14, allows users to control the speech and movement of a virtual avatar with their mind in real time. Boats have pulled up on the shore beside it, and their catches join the chaotic choreography inside, one plastic bucket at a time. pages.title: This Four-Person NASA Crew Spent Over a Year on 'Mars.' Here's What They Did for 378 Days in a Simulated Martian Habitat
pages.description: An intense selection process and long preparation helped set the crew up for cohabitation in a 3D-printed replication of the Red Planet's environment in Houston. There, they practiced Marswalks, disrupted communications with people on Earth and food cultivation
pages.text: This Four-Person NASA Crew Spent Over a Year on 'Mars.' Here's What They Did for 378 Days in a Simulated Martian Habitat Skip to main content Four individuals participated in NASA's second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission. NASA / James Blair On October 31, four NASA crewmembers returned from “Mars.” Not the actual Red Planet, of course, but a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston where the three men and one woman lived for 378 days. Now, the Mars analog astronauts— Ross Elder , Ellen Ellis , James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery —have started telling the world what took place after they disappeared into NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center on October 19, 2025, for the agency’s second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission. The mission aimed to test the kinds of physical and mental conditions that a team of Mars explorers would endure on the Red Planet, including long-term isolation, disrupted communication with people on Earth and food cultivation. The habitat includes both a base and a mock outdoor environment , so the crew could practice Marswalks. “For more than a year, they have lived in an isolated environment, conducting critical research and helping us better understand what it will take to send humans to Mars,” Vanessa Wyche , director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, said during a livestream , just before the crew emerged. “Inside just 1,700 square feet, they managed to live with limited resources. They maintained their habitat. They grew crops, and they carried out simulated Mars operations.”

pages.description: Design student Sneha Rao is developing Tact, an edible pregnancy test that allows people with vision impairment to feel its results on their tongues
pages.text: This Lollipop Could Help Blind Women Independently Detect Pregnancy Skip to main content The user, if pregnant, will feel raised bumps on both sides of the flat lollipop—a reaction to hCG, a hormone that the body produces during pregnancy. TACT Sneha Rao, a 27-year-old master’s student in design at Carnegie Mellon University, can trace the inspiration for her invention back to a 2020 article in the Wall Street Journal . In it, Eleanor Southwood, then the chair of the Royal National Institute of Blind People , said, “The dream is to buy any pregnancy test with the knowledge that it’s accessible.” A few years later, Rao came across a Newsweek article that talked about Joanne Hewitson, a blind woman whose TikTok went viral in 2024. “She talked about never being able to take a pregnancy test alone,” says Rao. As most pregnancy tests available on the market provide visual results, Hewitson has to depend on her sister to read the results for her. That article, says Rao, touched on something bigger than just pregnancy tests. “It was really about the systemic invisibility of blind and low-vision women in health care design more broadly,” she says. “That stuck with me, because it wasn’t just about the inconvenience,” explains Rao. “It was about moments where privacy is a safety need.” As Hewitson suggested: What if a blind person had no one they could trust to help them with a pregnancy test, or were in an abusive relationship? pages.text: This map shows where on Earth humans aren’t | National Geographic SCIENCE NEWS This map shows where on Earth humans aren’t A new map shows where people have the lowest impact—but are those the best places to protect? By Emma Marris Published June 5, 2020 • 6 min read A newly created map reveals the “wildest” places on Earth—places where humans have the lowest impact. The findings could be used to support the push to set aside half of Earth for nature , its authors say. “If you want to know where in the world you can find a place that has not yet been transformed by agriculture, infrastructure, or settlements, [this map] is where to find it,” says Erle Ellis, a global ecologist at the University of Maryland Baltimore County who contributed to the analysis. “There is a very strong consensus on where these places are.” The map, published today in the journal Global Change Biology, knits together four independently developed models for determining where humanity leaves its fingerprints, each using different indicators of activity. All four models use human population, built-up areas, and cropland as inputs, but then they start to specialize. The Global Human Footprint index also uses roads, railway lines, navigable waterways, night-time lights, and pasturelands to identify the places where humankind is least noticeable. The Heiltsuk (Haíɫzaqv) Nation, an Indigenous group, had set them up to capture destructive, invasive European green crabs. Sometimes the traps were destroyed. Other times their nets had been torn. Whoever raided the traps always went after the plastic bait cups, which held bits of herring or sea lion carcass. It looked like the work of wolves or bears, but many of the compromised traps stayed submerged during the low tide, so maybe sea otters? pages.description: A metal detectorist recovered the brass artifact from the wreck of the "Ann Francis," a merchant vessel that sank off southern Wales. Researchers used micro-CT scans to identify the four-letter combination
pages.text: This Mysterious Combination Lock Sank in a 1583 Shipwreck. When Engineers Cracked the Code, It Clicked Open for the First Time in More Than 400 Years Skip to main content The lock features four rotating dials, and each dial has six letters. Museum Wales In 1999, Peter Hughes stumbled upon the brass combination lock on Margam Beach in Wales. It featured four rotating dials, each bearing six letters. The dials turned smoothly, but only one of 1,296 possible combinations would open the device. The lock was an artifact from the Ann Francis , a merchant ship that sank in 1583. Hundreds of the vessel’s treasures—including compasses, coins and cannonballs—have since surfaced on the beach. But Hughes was particularly intrigued by the lock. He fiddled with the dials for two decades, trying to solve the puzzle. Now, researchers have used CT scans to reveal the four-letter code: ANCE. When they tested it out, the lock clicked open for the first time in more than four centuries. “For me, it’s like opening the Ark of the Covenant,” Hughes tells BBC Wales ’ Meleri Williams. “I’m delighted—truly thrilled.” The Ann Francis was traveling from Spain to England when a storm swept in on December 28, 1583. The winds blew it off course, and it ultimately wrecked off Margam Beach in southern Wales. According to a parish register, 14 sailors died in December 1583, and these men may have been the Ann Francis ’ crew. pages.title: This Odd-Looking New Spinosaurus Is Reviving an Age-Old Debate | National Geographic
pages.description: Could Spinosaurus swim? A new fossil with a scimitar-like head crest provides new evidence on the unsettled question.
pages.text: This Odd-Looking New Spinosaurus Is Reviving an Age-Old Debate | National Geographic SCIENCE This Odd-Looking New Spinosaurus Is Reviving an Age-Old Debate Could Spinosaurus swim? A new fossil with a scimitar-like head crest provides new evidence on the unsettled question. Unearthed in a rare Saharan fossil site in Niger, Spinosaurus mirabilis had a large head crest that may have signaled a message to rivals competing for resources or territory along the way. artwork by Dani Navarro By Helen Thompson Published February 19, 2026 Under the central Saharan sun, paleontologist Daniel Vidal spotted a mysterious bone poking out of the ground during an excavation in Niger. It looked like a dinosaur vertebra at first. But upon further inspection, researchers realized the bone was a curved, sword-like crest that would have been attached to the skull of one of paleontology’s most oddball dinosaurs—the sail-backed predator Spinosaurus . “It was amazing,” recalls Vidal, of the University of Chicago. “It was like a unicorn.” Back in 2022, when he stumbled upon the strange bone, he was part of a team led by National Geographic Explorer Paul Sereno, a paleontologist also at Chicago , excavating a remote fossil site called Jenguebi. Now, the researchers report the crest belonged to an entirely new species— Spinosaurus mirabilis —that roamed the area’s ancient river ecosystem some 95 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous. They published their discovery Thursday in Science . The new species adds to a heated debate over how these puzzling (and popular) dinosaurs lived and hunted in water.

Eighty percent of Americans live under a hazy umbrella of light pollution. Even if we put away the screens long enough to look up, the glare of our existence blocks out the stars . The good news? There’s a growing idea that wilderness extends to the skies. Parks, communities, and sanctuaries certified by the International Dark-Sky Association are slowly popping up all across the country. If approved, Colorado’s proposed 3,000-square-mile Sangre de Cristo International Dark Sky Reserve would be the world’s largest dark-sky designated area. Even without the designation, the skies of Southwest Colorado—shielded from the interstate glow by endless mountains—blaze with stars. So hop in the car. The harbour wall of Lyme Regis is also known as The Cobb. Thomas Faull, Getty Images By Jessica Prupas Published August 1, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Were you to dig below Lyme Regis’ bunting-slung streets, you’d hit a geological marvel: the Blue Lias. This vast sequence of limestone and shale layers, formed during the Mesozoic era some 200 million years ago, reveals fossils as it erodes, making the town one of Europe’s most important paleontological centres. pages.description: Tiger Woods is set to return to competitive golf in December for the first time in more than two years.
pages.text: Tiger Woods set for competitive golf return in December's Hero World Challenge - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Tiger Woods has won 15 major titles - three behind Jack Nicklaus' record tally By Timothy Abraham , BBC Sport Journalist and Michael Emons , BBC Sport journalist Published 4 hours ago Tiger Woods is set to return to competitive golf in December for the first time in more than two years. Woods, 50, has not played in a traditional ranking event since the 2024 Open Championship at Royal Troon amid a series of off-course issues. The 15-time major champion has endured a challenging few years with a number of injuries and turmoil in his personal life. Woods will host next month's Hero World Challenge - an event which is part of the PGA Tour schedule but does not carry FedEx Cup points - and has been announced as part of the 20-player field. The American is one of three exemptions for the tournament in the Bahamas along with compatriots Rickie Fowler and Gary Woodland. Speaking to SiriusXM PGA Tour Radio in a video posted last week, Woods said: "I'm feeling better, no doubt about that. "I've been training quite a bit. I will be at Hero either way, so I'll see you there." Woods' long-awaited return comes after he accepted a five-year driving ban in September following a plea agreement in his reckless driving case. In March, Woods had been arrested and charged with driving under the influence after clipping a truck and rolling his car in Florida.
